\chapter{Two Ways to Play, and Two Verbs That Bend}
\label{ch:it-play-get-answer}
\hlchaptermodality{21}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can tell apart the two Italian verbs English calls play — giocare for a game, suonare for an instrument — say that I obtain something and that I answer someone, and explain the silent h of giochi and the doubled tt of ottenere.}

The chapter's last lesson gathers gioco, suono, ottengo and rispondo, then reads risposto against preso: prehēnsum lost its n and gave preso, so respōnsum ought to have given risposo, and instead the verb joins the small -sto band with chiedere's chiesto — Chapter 17's rule that an irregular form is a regular one from a system you can no longer see.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[giocare, suonare]{giocare and suonare — the two verbs English calls \textquotedblleft{}play\textquotedblright{}}

\label{lesson:IT-C21-giocare}



\begin{quote}
English has one word for playing a game and playing an instrument. Italian has two unrelated ones, and picking the wrong one is the most recognisable mistake an English speaker makes.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: two words, not one}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{giocare} — to play a game, a sport, a match. \textbf{suonare} — to play an instrument; also, to ring or to sound.
\end{quote}

The line is what you are doing, not the English word:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{what you are doing} & \textbf{Italian} \\
\midrule
playing a game & \textbf{giocare} \\
playing an instrument & \textbf{suonare} \\
a bell ringing & \textbf{suona} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

Chapter 19 gave you the frame — \emph{mi piace} plus a dictionary form, as in \emph{mi piace leggere}:

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Mi piace giocare.} — I like playing. \textbf{Mi piace suonare.} — I like playing music.
\end{quote}

A grammatical tell too: \emph{giocare} wants \textbf{a} before the game's name, while \emph{suonare} takes the instrument bare.

\begin{cousinweb}
Two roots, never near each other.

\textbf{giocare} $\leftarrow$ Latin \textbf{iocārī}, \textquotedblleft{}to jest,\textquotedblright{} from \textbf{iocus}, \emph{a joke}. English took \emph{iocus} as \textbf{joke}, and through French as \textbf{jeopardy} — \emph{jeu parti}, \textquotedblleft{}a divided game.\textquotedblright{} Italian still calls a game \textbf{il gioco}.

\textbf{suonare} $\leftarrow$ Latin \textbf{sonāre}, \textquotedblleft{}to sound,\textquotedblright{} from \textbf{sonus}, \emph{a noise}. That is English \textbf{sound} itself, plus \textbf{sonata} (from Italian: a thing \emph{sounded}, against a \emph{cantata}, a thing sung), \textbf{resonate}, \textbf{unison}, \textbf{dissonant}. And \textbf{counterpoint} — Italian \emph{contrappunto}, note against note — carries the \emph{contrā} of the last lesson's \emph{incontrare} into music.

The split is no rule to memorise: two unrelated Latin words, covered in English by a single native verb.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: the h that keeps a c hard}]
Both are ordinary \emph{-are} verbs — until the \emph{tu} form of the first one.

\begin{quote}
\textbf{gioco, giochi, gioca} · \textbf{suono, suoni, suona}
\end{quote}

\emph{Gioco} is \emph{JO-ko}: the \textbf{g} is soft before \emph{i}, the \textbf{c} hard before \emph{o}. Now change the ending to \emph{-i}: written \emph{gioci}, that \emph{c} would soften to \emph{JO-chee}. Italian will not let a consonant shift because an ending did, so it spells in an \textbf{h}: \textbf{giochi}, \emph{JO-kee}.

You have met that letter doing opposite work:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{where} & \textbf{what the h does} \\
\midrule
\emph{chiedere}, \emph{mi chiamo}, \emph{giochi} & keeps a \textbf{c} hard before \emph{e} and \emph{i} \\
\emph{hanno} against \emph{anno} & separates two identical sounds in writing \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

The second row is Chapter 14: \textbf{hanno venti anni}, where \emph{hanno} (\textquotedblleft{}they have\textquotedblright{}) and \emph{anno} (\textquotedblleft{}year,\textquotedblright{} $\leftarrow$ \emph{annus}, the \emph{annus} of \emph{annual}) sound identical and only the silent \emph{h} tells them apart.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}gioco, giochi, gioca\textquotedblright{} · \textquotedblleft{}suono, suoni, suona\textquotedblright{}
  \item \textquotedblleft{}Mi piace giocare.\textquotedblright{} then \textquotedblleft{}Mi piace suonare.\textquotedblright{}
  \item the hard-c family — \textquotedblleft{}chiedere, mi chiamo, giochi\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which verb plays a match, and which an instrument? (\emph{Giocare}; \emph{suonare}.) Give each root and an English cousin. (\emph{Iocus} $\to$ \emph{joke}, \emph{jeopardy}; \emph{sonus} $\to$ \emph{sound}, \emph{sonata}.) Say you like playing music. (\emph{Mi piace suonare}.) Give the \emph{tu} form of \emph{giocare} and the letter's two jobs. (\emph{Giochi} — the \emph{h} holds the \emph{c} hard, as in \emph{chiedere}; in \emph{hanno} it separates the word from \emph{anno}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[ottenere]{ottenere — \textquotedblleft{}to get,\textquotedblright{} and a b that flattened into a t}

\label{lesson:IT-C21-ottenere}



\begin{quote}
The last lesson was about \textbf{doing} — playing a game, playing an instrument. This one is about \textbf{having}. English \emph{get} means almost anything; Italian has nothing of the sort, and for the sense that matters, \textbf{coming to have} a thing, the verb is this one.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: the word}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{ottenere} — to get, to obtain, to come to have.
\end{quote}

Line it up with what you have. \emph{Prendere} \textbf{seizes} a thing, \emph{portare} \textbf{carries} it. \emph{Ottenere} \textbf{obtains} it: it was not lying there for the taking.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{ottenere} comes from Latin \textbf{obtinēre}: \textbf{ob-}, \textquotedblleft{}toward, up against,\textquotedblright{} plus \textbf{tenēre}, \emph{\textquotedblleft{}to hold.\textquotedblright{}} To obtain is to get a hold on something:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{obtain} — the compound borrowed whole.
  \item \textbf{tenacious}, \textbf{tenant} and \textbf{tenure} (a holding), \textbf{tenet} (\textquotedblleft{}he holds\textquotedblright{}), \textbf{tenor}.
  \item \textbf{contain}, \textbf{retain}, \textbf{maintain} — which Chapter 17 gave you as \textquotedblleft{}hold in the hand.\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

English stacked prefixes on \emph{tenēre} exactly as it stacked them on the last chapter's \emph{portāre}: one Latin verb, a rack of prefixes.

\emph{Tenēre} also explains Chapter 14, where Italian counted years with \emph{avere}: \textbf{Ho venti anni}. \textbf{Spanish} says \emph{tengo veinte años}, \textbf{Portuguese} \emph{tenho vinte anos}, and both verbs are this same \emph{tenēre}. Where Italian \textbf{has} its years, Spain and Portugal \textbf{hold} theirs — and English and German simply \textbf{are} twenty.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: bt lands on tt, and a stem that bends}]
\emph{Obtinēre} has a \textbf{b} and a \textbf{t} side by side, and Italian will not say them that way. It does to \emph{-bt-} what it did to \emph{-ct-} and \emph{-pt-}: the first consonant flattens into the second.

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{Latin} & \textbf{Italian} \\
\midrule
\emph{octō} & \textbf{otto} \\
\emph{scriptum} & \textbf{scritto} \\
\emph{obtinēre} & \textbf{ottenere} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

The forms bend under stress: \textbf{ottengo, ottieni, ottiene}. A \textbf{g} surfaces in the \emph{io} form; the stem's \emph{e} breaks into \emph{ie} in the other two. Where \emph{giocare} spelled in an \textbf{h} to hold a consonant still, this verb lets the vowel move instead. The past is ordinary — \textbf{ottenuto}, regular the way \emph{portato} was, so \textbf{ho ottenuto}. That \emph{-ngo} is the shape Spanish shows in \emph{tengo}.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}ottengo, ottieni, ottiene\textquotedblright{} then \textquotedblleft{}Ho ottenuto.\textquotedblright{}
  \item the three — \textquotedblleft{}prendo, porto, ottengo\textquotedblright{}
  \item the clusters — \textquotedblleft{}\emph{octō} $\to$ otto, \emph{scriptum} $\to$ scritto, \emph{obtinēre} $\to$ ottenere\textquotedblright{}
  \item the years — \textquotedblleft{}Ho venti anni\textquotedblright{} beside Spanish \textquotedblleft{}tengo veinte años\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What two pieces make \emph{obtinēre}, and name three English cousins? (\emph{Ob-} plus \emph{tenēre}; \emph{obtain, tenacious, tenant, maintain}.) Why \emph{ottenere} and not \emph{obtenere}? (\emph{-bt-} flattens to \emph{-tt-}, as \emph{-ct-} did in \emph{otto}.) Give the singular forms and the participle, and the Chapter 20 participle it behaves like. (\emph{Ottengo, ottieni, ottiene}; \emph{ottenuto}, like \emph{portato}.) Which Latin verb do Spanish \emph{tengo} and Portuguese \emph{tenho} come from? (\emph{Tenēre}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[rispondere]{rispondere — \textquotedblleft{}to answer,\textquotedblright{} which is \textquotedblleft{}to pledge back\textquotedblright{}}

\label{lesson:IT-C21-rispondere}



\begin{quote}
Back to the \emph{-ere} family: the present costs nothing new. Chapter 19 taught you to ask; this is the other half, and its root is about a promise, not speech.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: the word}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{rispondere} — to answer. On the \emph{-ere} pattern of \emph{leggo} and \emph{chiedo}: \textbf{rispondo, rispondi, risponde}.
\end{quote}

One catch, mirroring one you own. \emph{Aspettare} takes its object bare where English needs a preposition — \emph{aspetto Anna}, \textquotedblleft{}I wait \textbf{for} Anna.\textquotedblright{} \emph{Rispondere} demands an \textbf{a} where English wants none:

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Rispondo a Marco.} — I answer Marco.
\end{quote}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{rispondere} $\leftarrow$ Latin \textbf{respondēre}: \textbf{re-}, \textquotedblleft{}back,\textquotedblright{} plus \textbf{spondēre}, \emph{\textquotedblleft{}to pledge solemnly.\textquotedblright{}} An answer was a pledge given in return, and the English family is unexpectedly personal:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{respond}, \textbf{response}, \textbf{responsible}; \textbf{correspond}, \textquotedblleft{}pledge together\textquotedblright{}; \textbf{despond}.
  \item \textbf{sponsor} $\leftarrow$ \emph{spōnsor}, who pledges for you.
  \item \textbf{spouse} $\leftarrow$ \emph{spōnsus}, \emph{spōnsa}, \textquotedblleft{}the promised one,\textquotedblright{} and \textbf{espouse}.
\end{itemize}

\emph{Chiedere}, with its hard \emph{ch}, came from \emph{quaerere}, \textquotedblleft{}to seek.\textquotedblright{} The asking-verb is a \textbf{hunt}; the answering-verb a \textbf{promise}.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: the participle, and which past a story uses}]
The participle is \textbf{risposto} — \textbf{ho risposto}, \textquotedblleft{}I answered.\textquotedblright{} Latin's was \emph{respōnsum}, with the same \emph{-ns-} as \emph{prehēnsum}, and \emph{prehēnsum} gave you \textbf{preso}: the \emph{n} dropped, a plain \emph{-s-} left. So this should be \emph{risposo}. It is not. \textbf{Risposto} joins a small \emph{-ere} band ending in \textbf{-sto}, with \emph{chiedere}'s \textbf{chiesto} — Chapter 17's principle over \emph{la mano}: an \textquotedblleft{}irregular\textquotedblright{} form is a regular one from a system you can no longer see.

Chapter 15's other past, the \textbf{passato remoto} — \emph{parlò}, \emph{parlarono} — is the one a story uses, because answering is what people do in stories. In Sicily and the south it is ordinary speech; in the north it retreated into books, as French shelved its \emph{passé simple}.
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built this chapter}]
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{giocare} $\leftarrow$ \emph{iocus}, \textquotedblleft{}a jest\textquotedblright{} $\to$ joke, jeopardy — a game. \textbf{suonare} $\leftarrow$ \emph{sonus}, \textquotedblleft{}a noise\textquotedblright{} $\to$ sound, sonata, unison — an instrument. English merged them; Italian never did.
  \item \textbf{ottenere} $\leftarrow$ \emph{ob-} + \emph{tenēre}, \textquotedblleft{}hold toward\textquotedblright{} $\to$ obtain, tenant, retain, with \emph{-bt-} landing where \emph{-ct-} and \emph{-pt-} did, and a bending stem: \emph{ottengo, ottieni, ottiene}.
  \item \textbf{rispondere} $\leftarrow$ \emph{re-} + \emph{spondēre}, \textquotedblleft{}pledge back\textquotedblright{} $\to$ respond, sponsor, spouse.
  \item \textbf{The thread}: Chapter 19 ended on verbs that \textbf{reach}, and on \emph{piacere}, which reaches back from the thing to you. This chapter closes it: \emph{ottenere} is the reach that lands, \emph{rispondere} the return journey, \emph{giocare} a reach for nothing at all.
\end{itemize}
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}rispondo, rispondi, risponde\textquotedblright{}
  \item \textquotedblleft{}Aspetto Anna\textquotedblright{}, then \textquotedblleft{}Rispondo a Marco\textquotedblright{}
  \item \textquotedblleft{}Ho risposto.\textquotedblright{} beside \textquotedblleft{}Ho chiesto.\textquotedblright{}
  \item \textquotedblleft{}gioco, suono, ottengo, rispondo\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Answer Marco. (\emph{Rispondo a Marco}.) What did \emph{spondēre} mean, and name three English cousins. (\textbf{To pledge}; \emph{respond, sponsor, spouse}.) Give the participle and say why it is not \emph{risposo}. (\emph{Risposto} — the \emph{-sto} band with \emph{chiesto}, not the \emph{-so} of \emph{preso}.) Which Latin verbs sit under \emph{chiedere} and \emph{ottenere}, and where is the \emph{passato remoto} everyday speech? (\emph{Quaerere}; \emph{tenēre}; \textbf{the south}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
